items.title: Jihad has greater and lesser meanings in classical Islam
items.claim: What is the greater/lesser jihad distinction?

options.text: Both refer only to armed warfare

A widely cited hadith distinguishes lesser jihad (armed struggle in defence of the community) from greater jihad (inner struggle against one's own ego); the hadith's authenticity is debated but the inner-struggle understanding is found in independent Sufi and mainstream piety traditions
Jihad refers only to economic struggle

items.reveal:
The Arabic root j-h-d means 'to strive, to exert effort'. The greater/lesser distinction is attributed to a hadith reported by al-Bayhaqi and al-Khatib al-Baghdadi: 'We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad — the jihad against the self.'

Ibn Taymiyya (d. 1328) and some modern scholars question the hadith's chain of authentication. But the inner-struggle theme appears widely in Sufi writing and is not dependent on the hadith alone.

Classical Islamic law (fiqh) regulates armed jihad with conditions on declaration, conduct, and protection of non-combatants — distinct from later extremist appropriations of the term.
items.why: A word picked up by 21st-century media can carry meanings that don't match its theological tradition. 'Jihad' in classical Islam is far more various than its English-language press usage.

items.title: Sikhism was founded in 1469 by Guru Nanak
items.claim: What was Guru Nanak's central teaching?

options.text: A synthesis of Hinduism and Buddhism

One God (Ek Onkar), equality of all people, honest work (kirat karna), sharing with others (vand chakna), remembrance of God (naam japna) — rejecting caste, ritualism and religious exclusivism of his time
A purely philosophical movement with no religious claims

items.reveal_title: There is neither Hindu nor Muslim
items.reveal:
Born in 1469 at Nankana Sahib (now in Pakistan), Nanak had a transformative spiritual experience in 1499. After emerging from three days at the Bein river he reportedly said 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim' — pointing past religious labels to a shared underlying truth.

He undertook four major journeys (udasis) across India, into Tibet, the Middle East and possibly to Mecca. He died in 1539.

The Mool Mantar — Sikhism's foundational statement — begins 'Ik Onkar': there is one God. The Guru Granth Sahib opens with this affirmation.
items.why: Sikhism is the youngest of the major Indian religions — a deliberate rethinking of religious identity in Mughal-era Punjab. Its founding moment is well-attested historically, unlike older religions.

items.title: Modern Judaism has Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and Reconstructionist branches
items.claim: What distinguishes the main Jewish denominations?

options.text: There are no real denominational differences

Orthodox (Modern Orthodox, Haredi), Conservative (Masorti in UK), Reform, and Reconstructionist — distinguished mainly by their stance on the binding nature of Halakhah (Jewish law) and engagement with modernity

items.reveal:
Reform Judaism emerged in early 19th-century Germany (Israel Jacobson, Abraham Geiger), arguing for adapting tradition to modern reason. Modern Orthodox (Samson Raphael Hirsch) defended strict observance of Halakhah while engaging modern life. Haredi (often called 'ultra-Orthodox') resists much of modernity.

Conservative/Masorti Judaism (Zacharias Frankel, Solomon Schechter at JTS New York from 1902) is a middle path — Halakhah binding but historically developing. Reconstructionist Judaism (Mordecai Kaplan, 1922) sees Judaism as an evolving religious civilisation.

In Israel the Chief Rabbinate is Orthodox and controls marriage and conversion law; in the US, Reform is the largest denomination by membership.
items.why: Religions are internally diverse. Judaism's denominational landscape sets up the central modern question — how do tradition and modernity relate? — in structurally different ways.
